questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a data management plan must specify
questions.learningObjective: name the decisions a data management plan has to settle in advance
questions.stem: A funder requires a data management plan before the grant starts. Which set of decisions genuinely has to be settled in that plan?

options.text: Formats, storage, naming, access, retention and destruction, so the data can still be found later
Sample size, power, exclusion rules and the planned test, since data planning is analysis planning
options.misconception: confuses managing data as an artefact with planning the statistical analysis

options.text: The research question, the literature review and the interview guide, since data planning covers the design
options.misconception: assumes a data management plan is the place to settle the study's design

options.text: The team list, the meeting calendar and the publication targets, since projects need administration
options.misconception: reads the plan as project administration rather than as a specification of the data

questions.explanation: A data management plan answers what will be produced, in what form, where it will live, what it will be called, who may see it, how long it will be kept and how it will finally be destroyed, and those are the decisions that determine whether the data can still be found and understood by someone who was not in the room. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why full anonymisation is often impossible
questions.learningObjective: explain why de-identification has a floor that no method crosses
questions.stem: A dataset records age, postcode district, rare condition and job title for 40,000 people. What should the team understand about anonymising it?

options.text: Combinations of ordinary attributes can single someone out, so the floor is reducing risk, not reaching zero
Removing the name column is sufficient, because no dataset can identify anyone without a name in it
options.misconception: believes direct identifiers are the only route to identifying a person

options.text: The dataset can be anonymised fully by replacing each value with a random number of the same length
options.misconception: assumes disguising the values removes them as a route to re-identification

options.text: Anonymisation is impossible for any dataset, so there is no point planning how much to reduce the risk
options.misconception: converts a limit on anonymity into a reason to make no effort at all

questions.explanation: Direct identifiers are the obvious route, but the quasi-identifiers matter just as much, because a person's age, the district they live in, a rare condition and an unusual job can combine to leave one plausible candidate in a whole country, and no amount of scrambling the values removes that. That is why de-identification is a standard to be met against a stated risk, with controlled access, aggregation and date coarsening where the combination is revealing, rather than a state to be achieved, and the trap is that removing the obvious column feels like finishing the job.
questions.hint: Ask what else besides a name could pick out one person.

questions.topic: Re-identification risk in a released dataset
questions.learningObjective: identify what makes a released dataset a re-identification risk
questions.stem: A funder asks for the study data to be released openly. Which feature of a dataset most directly creates re-identification risk?

options.text: Rare combinations of quasi-identifiers that leave very few candidates for some records
A large number of rows, since more records give an attacker more opportunities to guess
options.misconception: treats dataset size as the risk rather than the uniqueness of combinations

options.text: Values that have been rounded to the nearest year, since rounding is a form of alteration
options.misconception: treats any loss of precision as though it were a disclosure risk

options.text: A file format that any spreadsheet can open, since open formats spread the data further
options.misconception: blames the file format rather than what the records contain

questions.explanation: Risk comes from how many people share a given combination, so the damaging records are the ones where age, district, condition and job together leave almost nobody else, and those are found by counting how often each combination appears rather than by inspecting the file. questions.topic: What a data dictionary exposes
questions.learningObjective: explain what a data dictionary reveals about a dataset's internal consistency
questions.stem: A team writes a data dictionary and discovers the column called age allows values from zero to one hundred twenty. What has the dictionary done?

options.text: Made the intended meaning and range checkable, exposing records that contradict the stated definition
Described the file so that users need no documentation of any kind from the team again
options.misconception: assumes a dictionary removes the need to speak to the people who made the data

options.text: Repaired the column, so the out-of-range values no longer need any further attention
options.misconception: believes writing the definition also corrects the data it describes

options.text: Set the permitted range, so future entries outside zero to one hundred twenty will be rejected
options.misconception: treats documentation as though it were a validation rule enforced on input

questions.explanation: A dictionary is a claim about what each column means and what values it may legitimately take, and writing that claim down is what turns the data into something checkable, so the range it states is a test the file can fail and the age of one hundred and nineteen is now visible as a contradiction rather than as data. questions.hint: Ask what a stated range lets you discover in the file.

questions.topic: A sentinel number standing in for missing data
questions.learningObjective: explain why a numeric stand-in for missingness corrupts the data it stands for
questions.stem: A legacy file records every non-response as the number minus nine. Why is that a problem rather than a convenience?

options.text: The stand-in sits inside the real range, so a score that happens to equal it is deleted as if missing
The stand-in makes the file larger, so it takes longer to open and analyse than the original
options.misconception: treats the sentinel as a storage problem rather than a validity one

options.text: The stand-in hides which people did not answer, so the response rate cannot be reported at all
options.misconception: believes a sentinel removes the ability to count non-response rather than disguising it

options.text: The stand-in is fine, provided the analysis script removes the value before any mean is computed
options.misconception: assumes a later filter fully repairs a collision baked in at entry

questions.explanation: A sentinel is safe only when its value is one the real data can never take, and minus nine on a scale that can run that low is inside the range, so every genuine score of minus nine is thrown away by the very recode meant to tidy the file, and the loss is silent because a deleted row looks like a recoded row. File size and the ability to count non-response are untouched by the choice of code, and a later filter cannot recover a value already discarded, which is why the fix belongs at the point of entry rather than in the analysis.
questions.hint: Ask whether the real data could legitimately equal the stand-in.

questions.topic: A number stored as text
questions.learningObjective: explain what a text-stored number does to a column's arithmetic
questions.stem: One column of survey scores has a stray unit typed into some cells, so those cells hold text while the rest hold numbers. What follows?

options.text: Arithmetic on the column either errors or coerces the text to zero, quietly biasing any summary
The column is unusable for any purpose, so the survey has to be recollected from scratch
options.misconception: treats a storage-type fault as though it destroyed the collected responses

options.text: Only the mean is affected, so reporting the median instead of the mean would repair the column
options.misconception: believes a different summary statistic escapes a type fault in the underlying cells

options.text: Nothing changes, since a spreadsheet displays text and numbers identically in the same column
options.misconception: assumes identical display implies identical stored type and identical behaviour

questions.explanation: A column is one type or the other, and once some cells are text the whole column stops being reliably numeric, so a spreadsheet either refuses the average or reads the offending cells as zero and produces a mean that is too small, with no error message to say so. questions.topic: An ambiguous date and its consequence
questions.learningObjective: explain what an unstated date format does to a time series
questions.stem: A referral column holds values like the fourth of the fifth. What damage does the unstated format do, and what is the essential response?

options.text: Values that cannot exceed a month get misread as days, so ordering and elapsed time break silently
The dates are unreadable, so the whole column has to be deleted and the referrals re-collected
options.misconception: treats an ambiguous format as data that cannot be recovered at all

options.text: Only sorting is affected, so sorting the column before use is a sufficient correction
options.misconception: believes re-sorting repairs values that were already parsed the wrong way

options.text: The problem is cosmetic, since every reader knows which convention the column is meant to follow
options.misconception: assumes a shared convention exists in a file exchanged between teams

questions.explanation: Once a value such as the fourth of the fifth is parsed under the wrong convention it becomes a different and entirely ordinary-looking date, so the file no longer shows an error anywhere, the sequence quietly reorders and any interval computed from it is wrong, and the damage is discovered only if someone remembers that a day was never greater than twelve. Deleting the column, re-sorting it and relying on shared knowledge all leave the parsed values in place, which is why the format has to be fixed at entry and, for a file already exchanged, resolved against the source records before anything is analysed.
questions.hint: Ask what the software does with a day it does not recognise.

questions.topic: Finding a duplicate record
questions.learningObjective: identify the check that distinguishes a duplicate from a legitimate repeat
questions.stem: A patient appears three times in a referrals file. Which check separates an accidental duplicate from a real repeat visit?

options.text: Compare the whole row, since an accidental duplicate repeats every field while a real visit does not
Compare the file size, since duplicated rows always inflate the file beyond its expected length
options.misconception: looks for a whole-file symptom rather than testing the specific rows

options.text: Compare the patient's age at each visit, since ages cannot stay the same across a year
options.misconception: relies on a value that is unchanged across genuine repeat visits too

options.text: Compare the file's creation date, since duplicates are added later than genuine records
options.misconception: assumes a duplicate carries a distinguishable timestamp from a real record

questions.explanation: A repeated patient is expected, so the identifier cannot decide the question, and the test is whether every field matches, because a row re-sent by a faulty export or a double-clicked form repeats all of it while a genuine second visit carries a new date, a new referral reason and usually a new clinician. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An outlier that is valid
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an improbable valid record from a corrupted one
questions.stem: A wait time of nine hours appears in a clinic dataset where the rest fall under two hours. What is the right response?

options.text: Check it against the source record, since an extreme value can be entirely real and worth keeping
Delete it, since any value that far outside the range must be a data-entry error
options.misconception: equates improbability with invalidity and discards real cases

options.text: Replace it with the next highest value, so the distribution is not distorted by the extreme case
options.misconception: substitutes a near value for a possibly genuine one and hides the case

options.text: Keep it but report the mean both with and without it, so readers can judge the influence for themselves
options.misconception: treats a robust summary as an alternative to ever finding out whether the value is real

questions.explanation: An outlier is a value in an unusual tail, not a verdict on validity, and a nine-hour wait in an understaffed clinic is exactly the kind of case the study exists to describe, so the first move is to check the source record rather than to react to the number's position in the distribution. Deleting, substituting and reporting a robust summary all skip that check, and the trap is that removing extremes is one of the easiest ways to make a dataset look tidy and a finding look stronger than the evidence allows.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A transform applied twice
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of running a transform over an already transformed column
questions.stem: A script logs every column to which it applied a natural logarithm, then is re-run over its own output. What is the consequence?

options.text: The column is transformed a second time on already transformed values, so results no longer match the variable named
Nothing changes, because a logarithm of a logarithm is still a valid monotone transform of the original
options.misconception: believes any monotone transform is interchangeable for analysis purposes

options.text: The second pass is ignored, because scripts skip columns they have already transformed once
options.misconception: assumes scripts remember and avoid work they have already done

options.text: The column is restored to its original values, so a second pass simply undoes the first
options.misconception: assumes a transformation is reversible without the original value being kept

questions.explanation: A transform is a function applied to whatever is currently in the column, so re-running it over its own output does not cancel the first pass and does not get skipped, it produces a log of a log, which is a different and much less interpretable quantity than the log the analysis was planned around, and the column header still says the original. Calling it a valid monotone transform mistakes a property of the shape for a property of the analysis, and a script has no memory of its own earlier run unless one was deliberately built into it.

questions.topic: A spreadsheet formula that truncated
questions.learningObjective: explain why a stored formula is not a stored value
questions.stem: A column holds a spreadsheet formula that reaches into a lookup sheet. What is at risk in that arrangement?

options.text: The value exists only while the lookup is present, so a copy of the column alone is incomplete
The formula is slow to recalculate, so the analysis will run slowly but remain correct
options.misconception: reduces the risk to speed and overlooks what happens to the values

options.text: The column cannot be sorted or filtered, since spreadsheets refuse to reorder formulas
options.misconception: attaches a capability restriction to a real but unrelated spreadsheet limitation

options.text: Nothing is at risk, because the result is displayed in the cell exactly as a typed number would be
options.misconception: equates what a cell displays with what it contains

questions.explanation: A cell holding a formula holds an instruction rather than a number, so the number on screen is derived from a lookup that lives somewhere else, and any copy of the column that leaves the lookup behind arrives with instructions pointing at nothing, which is usually how a dataset turns into a file full of blanks. questions.hint: Ask what the cell contains rather than what it shows.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A hard-coded value that should be a parameter
questions.learningObjective: explain why a value written into code cannot be varied without editing it
questions.stem: A script contains a line filtering rows with a written-in threshold of 0.30. What does the hard-coded threshold prevent?

options.text: Running the same analysis at any other threshold, since the value cannot be varied without editing the code
The script from running at all, because a written-in value is not a legal expression
options.misconception: treats a hard-coded constant as a syntax error rather than a design limit

options.text: The threshold from being documented, since only parameters carry a description
options.misconception: believes a constant escapes documentation where a parameter would not

options.text: Nothing at all, since a threshold is a property of the data and not of the analysis
options.misconception: claims the analysis choice is fixed by the data rather than made by the analyst

questions.explanation: A threshold is an analytic decision, and writing it into the body of the script means the only way to see how results depend on it is to edit the file and run it again, so sensitivity checks become a sequence of manual edits with no record of which was used, and a reviewer cannot tell what was varied. A literal is perfectly legal, a constant is as documentable as a parameter, and whether a threshold is defensible is exactly what the choice should not be allowed to decide silently, which is the trap: the code reads cleanly and hides the decision inside it.
questions.hint: Ask what it would take to try a different value.

questions.topic: A script that depends on run order
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a hidden dependency on what the script ran before it
questions.stem: An analysis script works when run after a cleaning script and fails when run alone, with no error until the end. What is wrong?

options.text: It silently depends on an artefact left in the session by the other script, which is not in the archive
The machine is faulty, since a script that runs twice always fails the second time
options.misconception: attaches the behaviour to the machine rather than to a missing input

options.text: The script is too long, so its length is what causes the run-order dependency
options.misconception: links a hidden input dependency to code length

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since any competent user would know to run the cleaning script first
options.misconception: treats an undocumented dependency as resolved by the analyst's own habit

questions.topic: A random seed that was not recorded
questions.learningObjective: explain what an unrecorded seed costs a stochastic analysis
questions.stem: An analysis resamples 10,000 times using a random number generator whose seed was never written down. What has been lost?

options.text: The exact resamples, so the reported interval can be checked for consistency but not regenerated
Nothing, because the reported interval is a property of the data and not of the resampling
options.misconception: attributes the interval entirely to the data, ignoring the resampling that produced it

options.text: Only the speed of the computation, since a fixed seed is an optimisation rather than a requirement
options.misconception: treats seed recording as a performance concern rather than a provenance one

options.text: The validity of the method, since no interval from an unseeded run can be trusted at all
options.misconception: jumps from lost exactness to a verdict that the whole method is invalid

questions.explanation: A seed fixes the sequence the generator produces, and without it a re-run draws a different ten thousand resamples and returns a slightly different interval each time, so the procedure can be repeated in kind but not in fact, and a small discrepancy between two runs becomes impossible to interpret as noise or as a real change. The interval is not a property of the data alone, a fixed seed is about provenance rather than speed, and the trap is that the unseeded interval is not wrong, it is merely unfalsifiable, which is easy to overlook because nothing about it looks broken.
questions.hint: Ask whether a second run would return the same interval.

questions.learningObjective: diagnose an archive that cannot regenerate the reported analysis

Yes, because the deposited data already contains the cleaned and analysed version
options.misconception: assumes a deposited dataset includes the steps that produced it

options.text: Yes, because a written summary is enough for a competent analyst to reconstruct the steps
options.misconception: overstates what a narrative description guarantees for re-execution

questions.learningObjective: state what a preregistration does and does not bind

It has stopped the study, since public registration makes further data collection impermissible

options.text: It has guaranteed the result, since a registered plan makes the finding more likely to be correct

questions.topic: Exploratory versus confirmatory analysis
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an analysis that searches from one that tests
questions.stem: What separates an exploratory analysis from a confirmatory one?

options.text: A confirmatory test was specified before the data were seen, while an exploratory one lets the data pick the question
A confirmatory test uses a large sample, while an exploratory one works with a small sample
options.misconception: makes sample size rather than prior specification the dividing line

options.text: A confirmatory test uses numbers, while an exploratory one uses words and interview extracts
options.misconception: redefines the distinction as one of data type, which is the field's own fault

options.text: A confirmatory test is run once, while an exploratory one is run repeatedly until a result appears

questions.stem: A study asks adults to rate their pain while walking on a treadmill. How should minimal risk be judged?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A confirmatory test run on examined data
questions.learningObjective: classify an analysis correctly and say how it must be reported
questions.stem: A researcher examines the data, then tests the comparison that inspection suggested. First classify the test, then say how to report it.

options.text: Exploratory, and reported as such so that the prior look is not mistaken for a prediction
Exploratory, and reported as confirmatory because the test itself was run only once
options.misconception: lets the number of runs decide the status rather than the prior inspection

options.text: Confirmatory, and reported as confirmatory because the comparison was specified before the run
options.misconception: treats specification just before the run as though it were specification in advance

options.text: Confirmatory, and reported as confirmatory provided the result reaches significance
options.misconception: lets the outcome of the test settle whether it was confirmatory

questions.explanation: A test chosen after the data were seen has been shaped by that seeing, so its nominal error rate is optimistic and the honest label is exploratory, reported as such, and the reason the status has to be stated is that a reader cannot otherwise tell whether the comparison was a prediction or a discovery. Running it once, specifying it just beforehand and reaching significance are all facts about what happened afterwards, and the trap is that significance is the one thing a researcher wants to be able to report as confirmatory and so is the one thing that must not decide the question.
questions.hint: Ask when the comparison was chosen, not what it returned.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Minimal risk in a vulnerable group
questions.learningObjective: reach a defensible risk determination for a study in a dependent population
questions.stem: A team proposes to ask inpatients on a medical ward about a sensitive topic. First say what decides minimal risk, then say what extra question applies here.

options.text: The expected harm against daily life, and whether the ward's dependence could make agreeing feel compulsory
The expected harm against daily life, and whether the sample is large enough to estimate a proportion
options.misconception: introduces a precision criterion into a judgement about risk to participants

options.text: The number of inpatients exposed, and whether the topic has been asked on a ward before
options.misconception: judges risk by headcount and prior practice rather than by expected harm

options.text: Whether the findings would be anonymised, since anonymised answers cannot harm anyone
options.misconception: treats de-identification as settling whether participation is safe

questions.explanation: Minimal risk is settled by comparing the harm a reasonable person would expect with everyday life or routine examinations, and for inpatients there is a second question on top of that, because the person asking the questions may control their care, so agreement has to be secured in a way that cannot be read as compliance, and a patient who feels unable to refuse has been exposed to more than a sensitive questionnaire's ordinary risk. Sample size, prior practice on a ward and anonymisation each bear on other things, and the trap is that the risk discussion stays at the level of the topic and never reaches the relationship the participant is in.
questions.hint: Ask who is in a position to say yes to whom.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A truncated value and the figure built on it
questions.learningObjective: trace a precision fault from a stored value into a reported figure
questions.stem: An export stored every percentage to two decimals as text, so a share of 47.26 arrived as 47. First say what the export did, then say what that does to any total built from it.

options.text: It discarded precision that cannot be recovered, so any total is short and the loss is invisible in the file
It made the values text rather than numbers, so totals are unaffected but sorting is no longer available
options.misconception: assumes the storage type alone changes the values the totals are built from

options.text: It rounded the shares, which is harmless because rounding to two decimals is always acceptable
options.misconception: ignores that the discarded digits cannot be recovered from the file afterwards

options.text: It over-stated the shares, so totals run high and can be corrected by adding back the missing digits
options.misconception: gets the direction wrong and claims the precision survives in the file

questions.explanation: Rounding 47.26 down to 47 removes two digits that exist nowhere else, so a total built from a thousand such values is short by the accumulated loss and the file gives no way to detect it, since every cell looks like a deliberate two-decimal figure. The stored type matters for whether the column will sum at all, the rounding itself is not what changed the values, and the loss is downward rather than upward and cannot be added back, and the trap is that a two-decimal share looks like a chosen precision rather than a residual one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the original value can be rebuilt from what was stored.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A script that works only in one order
questions.learningObjective: diagnose and repair a hidden dependency between two scripts
questions.stem: An analysis script needs an object a cleaning script leaves in the session. First say what makes the dependency invisible, then say what removes it.

options.text: The object is never named or checked, and having each script create its own input removes it
The object is too large for the session, and compressing the data removes the dependency
options.misconception: attributes a missing-input problem to the size of the artefact

options.text: The script is long, and splitting it into shorter scripts removes the dependency
options.misconception: believes dividing the code also divides the data it silently reads

options.text: The cleaning script is separate, and merging the two into one file removes the dependency
options.misconception: hides the missing input inside a single file instead of naming it

questions.explanation: The dependency is invisible because the script never names what it reads, so it fails only when run in a fresh session, and only after doing most of its work, which puts the error a long way from its cause; the repair is for each script to construct or explicitly load its own input, so that a person can run it in any order and an archive can run it at all. Size, length and file layout are not what make the input disappear, and merging the scripts is the worst of the options because it hides the unnamed input inside a file that now looks self-contained.
questions.hint: Ask what the script reads that it never creates or loads by name.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why full anonymisation is often impossible
questions.learningObjective: explain the structural reason de-identification has a floor
questions.stem: A registry holds age, postcode district, a rare diagnosis and job title for every patient seen in a year. Explain why the team cannot make it fully anonymous, and what it can honestly claim instead.

answer.exemplar: Anonymity is not a property a file can be given by removing something, it is a claim about whether the remaining fields can single anybody out, and four ordinary-looking columns are enough because the disclosure happens in combination rather than in any one of them. A patient who is the only one of their age in a given district with a diagnosis that affects a few hundred people nationally and a job that few people hold can be narrowed to a very small number of candidates using nothing but the file plus public knowledge, and every field removed to reduce that risk is a field that might have supported a finding. So the honest claim is not full anonymity but de-identification to a stated standard, with the quasi-identifiers named, the combinations that leave very few candidates reported and either suppressed, coarsened or access-controlled, and the residual risk left visible rather than described as zero. That is a weaker promise and a usable one, whereas a claim of full anonymity is a promise the file cannot keep.

questions.explanation: A strong response says disclosure works through combinations rather than through any single field, so risk is reduced by named measures against a stated standard, and that the honest claim is a controlled residual risk rather than full anonymity.
questions.hint: Ask how many fields it takes before one person is picked out.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a seed belongs in the result
questions.learningObjective: explain what an unrecorded seed removes from a stochastic analysis
questions.stem: A study resamples its data ten thousand times and reports an interval, but never recorded the random seed. Explain what the missing seed costs and why it is not simply a matter of tidiness.

answer.exemplar: The seed fixes the sequence of draws the generator produces, so recording it fixes which ten thousand resamples were taken, and without it a re-run draws a different set and returns an interval that differs slightly every time, which means nobody can tell a difference caused by resampling from a difference caused by changed data or changed code. The interval is therefore not checkable, not wrong, and the cost is falsifiability rather than accuracy, which is why a missing seed does not show up as an error anywhere in the output. It matters most for the analyses whose whole point is that they are stochastic, since a bootstrap, a simulation and a random-forest result all depend on the draw, and a Bayesian analysis with a fixed seed can even report a convergence trace that has to be read the same way. The seed is a piece of the result, because the result includes the randomness, and a paper that reports it as an incidental implementation detail has recorded the part of the analysis that cannot be reconstructed.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the seed determines the draw, so without it the interval cannot be regenerated or compared, and characterises the loss as checkability rather than accuracy.
questions.hint: Ask what a second run of the same script would return.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a preregistration commits and how to depart from it
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of preregistration and what an honest departure looks like
questions.stem: A team registered a plan, then the data suggested a more interesting question. Explain what the registration does for the reader, and what the team should do now.

answer.exemplar: Registration is a dated public record of the decisions that were fixed before the data could influence them, and its value to a reader is that it converts an invisible claim about rigour into a checkable one, because the reader can compare the plan with the paper and see whether the outcome was tested or discovered. It binds the analysis rather than the topic, so a better question found later is a legitimate discovery and the honest response is to report it as a departure with a reason and a date, to present the registered result as well as the new one, and to say which analyses were exploratory, rather than quietly substituting the interesting outcome. Registering a second hypothesis and testing both is available where the journal permits it, and the version history of the registration shows when the plan changed, which is exactly the record a reader needs in order to judge how much of the result was anticipated. What a departure must never be is invisible, because an undisclosed change converts the protection the registration provided into decoration.

questions.explanation: A strong response says registration makes prior specification publicly checkable, that it binds the analysis rather than the topic, and that a departure must be reported with its reason, its date and the registered result alongside it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can compare the plan against.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a de-identification claim in a paper must cover
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a de-identification claim in a publication defensible
questions.stem: A paper says its released dataset is anonymised. Explain what that sentence would have to mean for it to be true.

answer.exemplar: For the sentence to be true rather than decorative, the paper would have to identify the direct identifiers that were removed, name the quasi-identifiers that were retained, and state what was done about the combinations of those that leave few candidates, because a claim of anonymity is a claim about the whole file's ability to single anybody out and the paper's one line is the only place a reader can check that. It would also have to say what was not done, since suppressing a rare diagnosis or coarsening a date to a year each removes analytic value and a reader assessing whether to use the data needs to know which were sacrificed, and would have to distinguish open release from release under a controlled agreement, because the same file can be safe for a public download and unsafe for a requester holding a rare-disease registry. What it cannot mean is that names were removed, and the phrase anonymised is worth distrusting precisely because it compresses a long series of specific decisions into one reassuring word.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the claim has to name the identifiers removed, the quasi-identifiers retained, the measures taken and the analytic value given up, and must separate open release from controlled access.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need to know to trust the word.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a reproducibility claim does and does not guarantee
questions.learningObjective: explain the exact scope of a reproducibility claim
questions.stem: A paper links its data, its code and a fixed environment file. Explain precisely what that establishes and where the claim stops.

answer.exemplar: What the deposit establishes is that the operations which produced the figures are written down in a form that can be executed, so the claim is about the completeness of the record rather than about the truth of the finding, and a reader who disagrees with the analysis can locate exactly where the disagreement lies and rerun it. A fixed environment file strengthens this by naming the versions the authors actually used, since code that relied on a behaviour later changed will otherwise fail or, worse, succeed with different numbers, so without it the guarantee is only that the code was once correct. The claim stops in three places. It stops at the inputs, because a data file that is deposited without the cleaning decisions does not let anyone reconstruct the raw data it was derived from. It stops at correctness, because re-running an analysis establishes that it can be repeated, not that it was the right analysis or that the finding is true. And it stops at durability, since licences expire, software archives disappear and repositories close, so reproducibility is a property of the deposit as it stands rather than a permanent one, and a claim of full reproducibility is strongest when it names all three boundaries.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the deposit concerns the completeness of the record, and separates the three things it cannot cover: the unrecorded cleaning steps, whether the analysis was appropriate, and whether the environment and licence will still hold.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader gains and what they still have to take on trust.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why an archive without a cleaning log cannot certify a result
questions.learningObjective: explain why the record of decisions matters as much as the data
questions.stem: A study deposits its raw data, its final analysis dataset and its code, but no record of how it got from one to the other. Explain what that gap costs.

answer.exemplar: The deposit contains the two ends of the work and nothing about the part between them, so every exclusion, recode, merge and derivation sits in a gap that the code and the final file do not fill, because the code operates on the final file and therefore takes the decisions as already made. Someone rerunning it reproduces the last step faithfully and has no way to check the ninety-nine that preceded it, and the reason this matters is that the steps taken between raw data and analysis file are exactly where a result is made, including the ones that are chosen with the outcome in view, which is why a dataset without its decision log cannot be audited for the kind of discretion the audit exists to detect. A second limitation compounds it, since the raw file is present but there is no declared link between it and the analysis file, so there is no way to confirm that every record removed was removed for a stated reason rather than an unstated one. The fix is unglamorous: a dated log naming each rule, how many rows it caught and the code version that applied it, which is a few hours of work at the point where the decisions are still fresh and impossible to reconstruct afterwards.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the deposit gives the inputs and the outputs but not the operations between them, that those operations are where discretion enters, and that the decisions cannot be reconstructed once nobody remembers them.
questions.hint: Ask what the code between the two files would need in order to run.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Detecting duplicate records
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that find and then classify duplicated records
questions.stem: A raw extract has arrived from a partner organisation. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Freeze a copy of the file exactly as received, and record its checksum
Group the rows by identifier, then inspect every group with more than one row
Compare the full rows within each group to separate exact repeats from real visits
Keep one copy of the true duplicates and record how many were removed
Log the decision, the rule and the count, so the removal can be re-checked

questions.explanation: The received file is preserved and checksummed first, because everything afterwards changes it and a check that cannot be run against the original is not a check. Rows are then grouped by identifier, which finds the repeats worth looking at without yet asserting that any of them is wrong, since a patient appearing twice is normal. Comparing the whole row within each group is what separates a genuine second visit, carrying a new date and reason, from a row sent twice, and only then is a copy removed and the count recorded. The decision, the rule that produced it and the number it caught go into the log, because a removal that leaves no record cannot be distinguished later from a record that was never present.
questions.hint: Preserve what arrived before deciding anything about it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: From raw file to analysis-ready data
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that take a raw extract to a defensible analysis file
questions.stem: Put these steps in the order that turns a raw extract into a file fit to analyse.

options.text: Preserve the file as received, with its checksum recorded
Check every column against the data dictionary before changing anything
Fix the format faults, including types and ambiguous dates, at the point of entry
Apply the cleaning rules once, from a written definition rather than by hand
Record each rule, the rows it touched and the count, then check the file again

questions.explanation: The order runs from protecting the evidence to proving the result of working on it. The file as received is preserved with a checksum, so any later version can be traced back and the check has something to be run against. The dictionary comes next, because a column cannot be judged until its intended meaning and permitted values are written down, which is what turns an odd value into a contradiction rather than a curiosity. Type and date faults are fixed at entry rather than downstream, since a value parsed wrongly once will be parsed wrongly by everything that follows. The cleaning rules are then applied from a written definition rather than by hand, so they can be re-run, and the last step records each rule with its row count and re-checks the file, which is what converts a claim that the data are clean into something an auditor can test.
questions.hint: Decide what the columns mean before deciding what is wrong with them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Preparing an archive for release
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that make a deposit verifiable and safe
questions.stem: A study is preparing its deposit. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Identify the direct and quasi-identifiers, and the combinations that leave few candidates
Remove or coarsen what the risk assessment says must go, or restrict access instead
Write the data dictionary, covering types, permitted ranges and every missingness code
Ship the code, the environment file, the seeds and the decision log with the data
Run the released analysis once from a clean machine and record what it produced

questions.explanation: The privacy work comes first because it changes what the file contains, and doing it after anything else means publishing and then retracting. The risk assessment names the identifiers and the combinations that leave few candidates, and the response may be removal, coarsening or a controlled-access agreement, all of which are legitimate and which the paper then has to describe honestly. The dictionary comes next, because a de-identified file is unusable if nobody can tell what a value means, and the seeds, environment and decision log ship with the code so the deposit records the analysis rather than only its output. The last step is the one that makes the claim checkable: running the released analysis on a clean machine and recording the output is the only way to find out whether the deposit actually works before someone else finds out for you.
questions.hint: Decide what may be released before deciding what goes in the release.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Running and reporting a preregistered analysis
questions.learningObjective: sequence a confirmatory analysis and its reporting
questions.stem: A preregistered analysis is about to be run. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Apply the registered exclusions without re-examining the outcome data
Run the registered model with the registered covariates, exactly as specified
Report the estimate with its interval, whatever the direction or the significance
State the result beside the registration, showing the analysis matched the plan
Label anything added afterwards as exploratory, with the date and reason it was added

questions.explanation: The registered exclusions are applied without looking at the outcomes, because an exclusion inspected against the results is a new decision dressed as an old one, and then the model runs as specified, with the covariates and the outcome the plan named. The estimate and its interval are reported whichever way they point, since a registration that is only honoured when it is agreeable is worth nothing, and the result is placed beside the registration so a reader can see the match directly. Whatever was added afterwards is then labelled exploratory with the date and reason, which is the only place a later idea can be honestly recorded without passing itself off as the plan.
questions.hint: Decide what goes into the analysis before seeing what comes out of it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A de-identification claim backed by a uniqueness count
questions.learningObjective: interpret a de-identification report that states its own risk measure
questions.stem: A release reports that 14 of 20,000 records are unique on age, district and sex, and declares the file anonymised. What is the fair reading?

options.text: Fourteen people remain individually pickable, so the file is de-identified with a named residual risk
The file is fully anonymous, because fourteen out of twenty thousand is a negligible share
options.misconception: judges disclosure by the share of records rather than by who is exposed

options.text: The release is unusable, because any uniqueness at all makes a dataset unsafe to publish
options.misconception: treats a named residual risk as though it disqualified the whole release

options.text: The count proves no risk remains, since unique records are the only ones that identify anyone
options.misconception: assumes uniqueness on the three named fields settles identification entirely

questions.explanation: Risk falls on the fourteen people who are uniquely pickable, not on the file in proportion, and a release that names the count, names the fields and says what it did about them is making a defensible claim, which is that the data were de-identified to a stated standard with fourteen identified individuals left. A negligible share, a total bar on uniqueness and a count presented as proof of safety each misread what a uniqueness check is, and the trap is that a small number is genuinely reassuring about the file and genuinely bad news about the fourteen, and only the second half of that is about people.
questions.hint: Ask who the risk lands on, not how much of the file it covers.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A reproducibility claim the archive does not support
questions.learningObjective: check a reproducibility claim against the deposited archive
questions.stem: A paper states the analysis is fully reproducible. The deposit holds an analysis-ready file and a script that reads it, but no code that produced it. What follows?

options.text: The steps between the raw data and the file are missing, so the analysis runs but cannot be checked
The claim holds, since re-running the script on the deposited file does reproduce the figures
options.misconception: accepts reproducing the final step as though the whole analysis had been reproduced

options.text: The claim holds, since the deposited file is itself the cleaned and prepared dataset
options.misconception: mistakes an intermediate artefact for a record of the operations that created it

options.text: The claim fails entirely, since no deposit can ever make an analysis reproducible
options.misconception: jumps from one missing piece to a verdict that the goal is unattainable

questions.explanation: The deposit proves the last step, because the script plus the file will regenerate the figures, and it says nothing about every exclusion, merge and derivation that produced the file, which is where a result is actually made and where discretion enters, so the reproducible part is the part that was already settled. A cleaned file is not a record of the cleaning, and a claim of full reproducibility is not refuted by a missing script so much as narrowed to what was deposited, and the trap is that the test a reader will actually run, running the code, passes, which is precisely why the gap can go unnoticed.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the process the deposited code covers.
